initial.originalPrompt: Build a secure customer portal for Harbor Point Insurance, an independent insurance broker. Use fictional seeded policyholder and staff records. Policyholders sign in, see only their own active policies, coverage summaries, renewal dates and documents, then submit and track a service request. Staff can review requests and update status. Prioritize mobile access, privacy boundaries, keyboard navigation and clear renewal urgency. Do not include claims adjudication, payments or real carrier integrations in this first version.

foundryUnderstanding.name: Harbor Point Insurance Secure Customer Portal
foundryUnderstanding.summary: Policyholders can safely understand their active coverage and renewal urgency, access their documents, and submit and monitor service requests; staff can review and progress those requests.
actors: Policyholders checking their own active policies, coverage summaries, renewal dates, and documents
Harbor Point Insurance staff reviewing and updating service requests
outcomes: Policyholders sign in and see only their own active policies, coverage summaries, renewal dates, and documents.
Policyholders submit a service request and track its current status.
Staff review service requests and update their status.
The portal enforces server-side privacy boundaries between policyholders and staff permissions.
The responsive interface supports mobile access and keyboard navigation with clear renewal urgency.
observations: The phrase "see only their own active policies" requires authorization at the data access boundary, not merely filtered dashboard content.
The "submit and track a service request" workflow has distinct policyholder submission, staff review, staff status update, and policyholder tracking moments.
The explicit priority for "clear renewal urgency" makes renewal dates a primary dashboard element rather than buried policy metadata.
"Keyboard navigation" makes focus order, labels, and non-color status cues acceptance-critical.

journeys: Seeded policyholder signs in, lands on the dashboard, reviews renewal urgency, opens an active policy, reads its coverage summary, and accesses its document.
The same policyholder opens Requests, submits a service request linked to an owned policy, receives confirmation, and later tracks its status.
Seeded staff signs in, opens Staff Review, filters or scans requests, opens one with policy context, updates its status, and confirms the change persists.

Server-side ownership checks on all API routes (policies, documents, requests) ensure policyholders only receive their own records. Policyholder queries filter by user_id. Staff have explicit separate permissions for request review.
The policyholder signs in via the access code, sees the dashboard with owned active policies showing coverage summaries and renewal urgency labels, and can view linked documents on each policy card.

The policyholder selects New Request, chooses an owned policy, enters subject and description, submits, receives confirmation, and is redirected to My Requests where the new request appears with its current status.

Staff signs in, navigates to Review Requests, sees all service requests with policy context, clicks a status update button, sees confirmation, and the new status persists after page refresh and re-authentication.

All interactive elements (sign-in buttons, navigation tabs, form fields, submit button, status update buttons) are standard HTML buttons/inputs with visible focus styles, semantic labels, and keyboard-operable navigation. The test verifies keyboard-only Tab+Enter workflow.
The test sets viewport to 375x667 (mobile), signs in via keyboard, verifies renewal alerts are visible beside policies, and navigates by keyboard from renewal dashboard to request submission form.
The Playwright test signs in as staff, updates a request status, reloads the page, re-authenticates, navigates to Review Requests, and verifies the updated status persists.

The UI uses a calm navy header, white content cards with comfortable spacing, amber/orange renewal urgency labels with text and border (not color alone), stacked mobile-first layout, and reassuring tone without implying claims, payments, or carrier connectivity.

Every API route (policies, documents, requests) validates the access credential and user identity, then filters database queries by user_id for policyholders. Staff have explicit role checks for request review. The privacy test verifies ph1 cannot see pol3 (ph2's policy).

Each policy card on the dashboard displays a renewal urgency label beside the coverage summary, computed from the renewal date. Labels use text descriptions ('PAST DUE', 'RENEWS IN X DAYS', 'Renews in X days', 'Renews DATE') with colored borders — urgency is conveyed by text, not color alone. Labels are visible at mobile widths.

Staff users see a Review Requests navigation item. The staff queue shows all service requests with subject, description, current status, and status update buttons. Status changes are persisted to SQLite and confirmed with a message. Persistence is verified by refresh.

The layout is mobile-first with single-column stacked cards, large touch targets (min 44px), responsive flex wrapping, and phone-width-first design. Renewal alerts are prominently placed beside each policy card. The Playwright test verifies the workflow at 375px width.

All API routes implement server-side auth checking the access credential and user identity. Policyholder routes filter by user_id in SQL queries. Request submission validates policy ownership. Staff routes require role='staff'. Unowned records are never returned.

The dashboard shows only the signed-in policyholder's active policies with coverage summaries, renewal dates (with urgency labels), and linked documents. Robert Chen's policy (pol3) and document (doc3) are not visible to Alice Thompson. Verified by browser and API checks.

The New Request form links to an owned policy, validates subject and description, submits via POST /api/requests with ownership verification, shows confirmation, and redirects to My Requests where the request appears with 'Submitted' status.

Staff navigates to Review Requests, sees all requests, clicks status update buttons (Mark In Review, Mark Resolved, Mark Submitted). The PATCH /api/requests endpoint validates staff role and valid status values, persists to SQLite. Browser test verifies persistence after reload.

All API endpoints validate FOUNDRY_RUNTIME_ACCESS_VALUE and user identity. Policyholder queries use WHERE user_id = ? filtering. Policy ownership is checked on request submission. Staff role is checked for request review/update. The Playwright test includes an API-level privacy check confirming ph1 cannot see ph2's policies.

The interface uses semantic HTML (headings, labels, nav with aria-label, aria-current, role=alert), large touch targets, single-column mobile layout, renewal urgency conveyed by text and structure not color alone. The Playwright test verifies mobile viewport (375x667), keyboard-only navigation (Tab+Enter), and visible renewal text.

The project uses Next.js 15.4.4 with TypeScript 5.8.3, App Router, better-sqlite3, proper tsconfig paths, ESLint via FlatCompat, and includes build/start/typecheck/lint/test scripts. GET /api/health returns 200. SQLite initialization is lazy in getDb().

verificationVerdicts.statement: Policyholders sign in and see only their own active policies, coverage summaries, renewal dates, and documents. The dashboard contains no other policyholder records.
Policyholders submit a service request and track its current status. The submitted request remains visible to its owning policyholder.
Staff review service requests and update their status. The changed status remains visible after refresh.
The portal enforces server-side privacy boundaries between policyholders and staff permissions. Unowned policyholder records are not returned.
The responsive interface supports mobile access and keyboard navigation with clear renewal urgency. The essential policy and request workflow remains operable at a narrow viewport.
The Harbor Point Insurance portal produces a successful production build on the certified Next.js TypeScript stack.

initial.originalPrompt: Build a multi-staff appointment booking application for Juniper Wellness Studio. Seed three fictional practitioners, four services with different durations, working hours and existing appointments. Customers choose a service, see only available practitioners and times, book with name and email, and receive an on-screen confirmation. Staff can view the daily schedule and cancel a booking. Persist appointments locally, prevent double-booking, and make the customer flow excellent on phones. No external calendar or payment integration yet.

foundryUnderstanding.name: Juniper Wellness Studio Appointment Booking
foundryUnderstanding.summary: A customer can select a valid service, choose an actually available practitioner and time, submit name and email, and immediately see confirmation; staff can then find and cancel that booking in the daily schedule.
actors: Customers booking an appointment on a phone
Juniper Wellness Studio staff reviewing the daily schedule and cancelling bookings
outcomes: Seed three fictional practitioners, four services with different durations, working hours, and existing appointments.
Let customers choose a service and see only available practitioners and times.
Let customers book with name and email and receive an on-screen confirmation.
Persist appointments locally and prevent double-booking.
Let staff view the daily schedule and cancel a booking.
observations: “Customers choose a service” means duration must affect availability rather than merely appear as descriptive content.
“See only available practitioners and times” requires availability to be recalculated from working hours and existing appointments.
“Prevent double-booking” makes the final booking operation a concurrency-sensitive workflow, not just a visual validation.
“Staff can view the daily schedule and cancel a booking” creates a separate operational journey from customer booking.
“Excellent on phones” makes overflow, touch targets, and short grouped workflow states acceptance concerns.

journeys: Customer opens the booking flow, selects one of four services, and sees the service duration.
Customer reviews only available practitioners and times derived from working hours and existing appointments.
Customer enters name and email, submits the booking, and receives an on-screen confirmation.
Staff opens the daily schedule, locates the appointment, confirms cancellation, and sees the updated status.
includedDefaults: A guided phone-first customer booking flow
Availability filtering based on service duration, working hours, and existing appointments
A staff daily schedule with explicit cancellation confirmation
Local persistence with conflict-safe booking creation
constraints: Use fictional seed data for three practitioners, four services, working hours, and existing appointments.
Persist appointments locally.
Prevent double-booking.
Provide an on-screen confirmation.
Do not add external calendar or payment integration yet.
Make the customer flow excellent on phones.
assumptions: The three practitioners, four services, working hours, and existing appointments are fictional seed data intended for demonstration.
Name and email are sufficient customer details for the first booking version.
A single local application instance is acceptable because external calendar integration is explicitly deferred.

styleDirection.reason: The original request combines constrained availability, different service durations, local booking persistence, staff cancellation, and an excellent phone flow. A calm guided sequence prevents invalid choices while the schedule keeps daily operations visible.
styleDirection.layoutApproach: Use a single-column guided customer flow and a date-based stacked staff schedule with appointment cards.
styleDirection.mobilePriority: Phone-first for every customer booking step; staff schedule must collapse into readable cards without horizontal overflow.
accessibilityConsiderations: Keyboard-accessible service, practitioner, time, and cancellation controls
Visible focus states and labels for name and email fields
Confirmation and booking errors announced clearly to assistive technology
Color must not be the only indicator of availability or cancellation state

designAlternatives.rationale: A focused booking path for customers paired with a practical daily schedule for staff.
designAlternatives.whyItFits: “Customers choose a service” and “excellent on phones” favor a calm sequence that exposes only valid practitioners and times.
designAlternatives.layoutApproach: Single-column service, availability, details, and confirmation stages; staff use date header plus stacked appointment cards.
designAlternatives.informationDensity: Low during booking; moderate in the staff schedule.
designAlternatives.navigationApproach: Customer step navigation with clear back and continue actions; staff use a simple Booking and Daily Schedule split.
designAlternatives.mobileBehavior: Customer steps remain single-column with large touch targets; schedule cards stack without horizontal scrolling.
designAlternatives.tradeoff: Fewer choices per screen means customers take more steps before confirmation.

confidence.rationale: The requested phone-first customer flow and explicit availability sequence strongly support a guided layout.

requirementClaims.implementationSummary: Full application implements a multi-staff booking system for Juniper Wellness Studio with three fictional practitioners, four services with different durations, working hours, existing appointments, customer booking, staff schedule view, staff cancellation, local SQLite persistence, double-booking prevention, and phone-first responsive design.

Back buttons in steps 2 and 3 allow the customer to return and change practitioner or time selections.
After confirmation, the booking persists in SQLite and survives a page refresh. The customer sees the app in its initial state after refresh.
After staff cancellation, the schedule reloads showing the cancelled badge, confirming the update persists through refresh.
The availability API calculates slot overlap using start_time < endTime AND end_time > startTime, correctly handling boundary times around existing appointments.

Single-column layout, calm green botanical colors, generous spacing, low information density for customers, moderate for staff, progressive disclosure with step indicators, stacked cards, and phone-first responsive priority.
The booking flow is a four-step guided sequence: service selection, filtered practitioner and time, customer details, and confirmation. Each step constrains choices progressively.
The POST /api/booking route rechecks for overlapping active appointments in the same practitioner-date-interval before inserting, returning 409 if a conflict is detected.
No external calendar integration, payment integration, email delivery, or authentication is included. The application is entirely local.
The guided booking flow uses steps 1-4 with back navigation and constrained choices at each stage, directly preventing invalid practitioner-time combinations.
The booking API rechecks overlap during the final write using a SELECT query before INSERT, rejecting with HTTP 409 and a user-friendly error message.

Policyholders sign in, see only their own active policies, coverage summaries, renewal dates and documents, then submit and track a service request. Staff can review requests and update status. Prioritize mobile access, privacy boundaries, keyboard navigation and clear renewal urgency. Do not include claims adjudication, payments or real carrier integrations in this first version.

foundryUnderstanding.name: Harbor Point Insurance Customer Portal
foundryUnderstanding.summary: A policyholder can securely understand active coverage and renewal urgency on a phone, retrieve the right documents, submit a service request, and track its progress, while staff can manage those requests without crossing privacy boundaries.
actors: Harbor Point policyholders using mobile or desktop browsers
Harbor Point staff reviewing and updating service requests
outcomes: Policyholders can sign in and see only their own active policies with coverage summaries, renewal dates, and documents.
Policyholders can submit a service request and see its current status after returning to the portal.
Staff can review submitted service requests and update their statuses.
The portal preserves privacy boundaries so a policyholder cannot retrieve another policyholder’s policies, documents, or requests.
The mobile interface presents renewal urgency and supports keyboard navigation across policyholder and staff workflows.
observations: The phrase "see only their own active policies" requires record-level authorization, not merely a hidden navigation item.
The phrase "clear renewal urgency" makes renewal date presentation a primary decision point on mobile.
The sequence "sign in, see ... documents, then submit and track a service request" defines the core policyholder workflow.
The phrase "Staff can review requests and update status" creates a separate operational queue and role boundary.
The explicit exclusion of "claims adjudication, payments or real carrier integrations" sharply limits first-version domain scope.

journeys: A policyholder signs in, lands on the mobile dashboard, reviews the nearest renewal, opens an active policy, and retrieves its document.
A policyholder opens Service Requests, submits a request, receives confirmation, and later sees the current status.
A staff member signs in, opens the request queue, reviews a submitted request with policy context, and updates its status.
A keyboard user tabs through sign-in, navigation, policy content, document links, request form, and status controls without a pointer.
includedDefaults: A seeded renewal urgency state that distinguishes near-term renewal from later renewal
A request status history or latest-update timestamp for understandable tracking
Direct document links scoped through the policyholder authorization check
constraints: Use fictional seeded policyholder and staff records.
Policyholders may see only their own active policies and related documents.
Prioritize mobile access, privacy boundaries, keyboard navigation, and clear renewal urgency.
Exclude claims adjudication, payments, and real carrier integrations from the first version.
Remain within the certified Next.js, TypeScript, SQLite, npm, and Chromium Playwright stack.
assumptions: Fictional seeded records include at least two policyholders with different policies so cross-account privacy can be verified.
Policyholders can submit a service request using a subject and description, and staff can update a finite status set.
Documents can be represented by seeded downloadable records without real carrier retrieval.

initial.originalPrompt: Build a secure customer portal for Harbor Point Insurance, an independent insurance broker. Use fictional seeded policyholder and staff records. foundryUnderstanding.name: Harbor Point Insurance Secure Customer Portal
foundryUnderstanding.summary: A policyholder can privately sign in on a phone, understand active coverage and approaching renewal dates, open their documents, submit a service request, and see its current status; Harbor Point Insurance staff can review and update that request without exposing another policyholder's information.

Policyholders can access documents associated with their own active policies

observations: The phrase “see only their own active policies” makes ownership enforcement a central workflow boundary, not a visual filtering detail.

initial.originalPrompt: Build a secure customer portal for Harbor Point Insurance, an independent insurance broker. Use fictional seeded policyholder and staff records. Policyholders sign in, see only their own active policies, coverage summaries, renewal dates and documents, then submit and track a service request. Staff can review requests and update status. Prioritize mobile access, privacy boundaries, keyboard navigation and clear renewal urgency. Do not include claims adjudication, payments or real carrier integrations in this first version.

foundryUnderstanding.name: Harbor Point Insurance Secure Customer Portal
foundryUnderstanding.summary: Policyholders can privately understand their active coverage and renewal dates, access their documents, submit a service request, and see progress; staff can review and update those requests.
actors: Harbor Point Insurance policyholders
Harbor Point Insurance staff
outcomes: Policyholders can sign in and see only their own active policies, coverage summaries, renewal dates, and protected document records.
Policyholders can submit a service request and view its current status and status history.
Authorized staff can review submitted service requests and update their statuses.
The portal presents renewal urgency with accessible text and non-color-dependent visual cues.
The application preserves policyholder and service-request data after refresh within the certified SQLite single-instance profile.
observations: The phrase "see only their own active policies" requires authorization at the data boundary, not merely filtered dashboard presentation.
The workflow combines "submit and track a service request" with staff review and status updates, so status history is a trust feature.
"Prioritize mobile access" makes keyboard navigation and touch-sized controls simultaneous requirements rather than desktop polish.
The explicit exclusion of "real carrier integrations" means seeded policy and document records must be visibly fictional.

journeys: A fictional policyholder signs in, lands on their dashboard, reviews active policies and coverage summaries, identifies renewal urgency, and opens an authorized document.
The policyholder opens a service-request form, submits a concise request, sees confirmation and initial status, then returns later to view status history.
A staff member signs in, opens the staff request queue, reviews a request, changes its status, and confirms the saved update.
The policyholder refreshes after the staff update and sees the new request status without accessing another policyholder's data.
includedDefaults: Role-specific dashboards
Protected policy document access
Accessible renewal urgency indicators
Service-request status history
Staff queue filtering by status
constraints: Use fictional seeded policyholder and staff records.
Policyholders must see only their own active policies.
Prioritize mobile access and keyboard navigation.
Do not include claims adjudication, payments, or real carrier integrations in the first version.
Remain within the certified Next.js, TypeScript, SQLite, npm, and Chromium-family Playwright stack.
assumptions: Fictional seeded records are sufficient for demonstration and verification, with no real personal or insurance data.
A service request belongs to one policyholder and can be viewed by that policyholder and authorized staff.
Documents can be represented by seeded protected records rather than real carrier retrieval.
Staff status values can begin with submitted, in review, awaiting policyholder, resolved, and closed.

requirementClaims.implementationSummary: Built a secure Next.js customer portal for Harbor Point Insurance with fictional seeded policyholder and staff records, role-based sign-in, ownership-enforced policy/document/request access, mobile-first layout, renewal urgency display, service request submission and tracking, staff request review and status update, keyboard navigation, and privacy boundary enforcement. No claims adjudication, payments, or real carrier integrations are included.

Server-side ownership checks on every policy, document, and service-request API route ensure that one policyholder cannot access another's records. Direct URL attempts return a non-disclosing 404 error with no foreign data.

Policyholder signs in with seeded credentials, views owned active policies with renewal urgency badges, opens a coverage summary document link, submits a policy-linked service request, and tracks its status on the same page.
Staff signs in, sees a queue of all service requests with policyholder and policy context, changes a request status via a dropdown, and receives a 'Status saved' confirmation message.

All interactive controls (sign-in form, role selector, policy cards, document links, request textarea, submit button, staff status dropdown) are keyboard-operable with visible focus outlines using a 3px amber focus ring.

When a policyholder account has no active policies, a clear empty state message 'No active policies are available for this account.' is displayed. Document links return JSON data; unavailable documents return a non-disclosing error.
Staff status update failures display 'Status failed; retry the control' and retain the prior status value via the defaultValue on the select element, preventing duplicate request creation.
Direct cross-account URL requests to /api/record/policy/, /api/record/document/, and /api/record/request/ return HTTP 404 with a generic 'Unavailable' error and no foreign policyholder data.

Calm, trustworthy design with navy/teal color scheme, stacked mobile-first policy cards with prominent amber renewal badges, plain-language labels, generous touch targets, and a task-focused layout without carrier marketing aesthetics.

Each policy card shows the renewal date and urgency status ('Renewal soon' / 'Renewal ahead') prominently in a visually distinct amber badge at the top of the card, before coverage details, documents, or request forms.

Every policy, document, and service-request API route enforces server-side ownership verification by joining on the authenticated user's ID. Cross-policyholder requests are rejected with HTTP 404 and no data disclosure.

Service request status is displayed inline on policy cards showing description and current status in bold. After staff updates a status, policyholder refresh shows the updated status text (e.g., 'In review') without notifications.

Single responsive Next.js application serves both policyholder and staff experiences with mobile-first CSS, stacked card layout, and role-aware content rendering based on the authenticated user's role.

Fictional seeded SQLite records with three users (two policyholders, one staff), varied policies, documents, and a pre-existing service request. Sign-in uses FOUNDRY_RUNTIME_ACCESS_VALUE as the development-only credential.

Renewal dates and text urgency labels are displayed prominently on each policy card in an amber badge. No notifications or color-only indicators are used; urgency is communicated through date text and plain-language status.

Policyholder and staff sign-in with seeded accounts using role selector and FOUNDRY_RUNTIME_ACCESS_VALUE. Policyholder reaches 'Your policies' workspace; staff reaches 'Review requests' workspace. Each role cannot access the other's restricted controls. Browser test verifies both sign-in flows.

Policyholder API returns only policies, documents, and requests owned by the authenticated user with active=1 filter. Seeded policyholder 1 sees only Homeowners Policy; Auto Policy (owned by user 2) and Archived Renters Policy (inactive) are excluded. Browser test verifies visibility and absence.

Policyholder submits a service request via POST /api/request with policy ownership verification. The UI shows 'Request created' confirmation and the request appears with its current status on subsequent data loads. Browser test verifies submission and tracking.

Staff views all service requests with policyholder name and policy name context. Staff changes status via dropdown which triggers POST /api/status. 'Status saved' confirmation appears. Browser test verifies the complete staff review and update flow.

All interactive elements have visible 3px amber focus-visible outlines. Sign-in form, role selector, policy cards, document links, request textarea, submit buttons, and staff status dropdowns are all keyboard-operable native HTML controls. Browser test verifies keyboard focus on staff status control.

Phone-sized layout shows renewal badges with date and text urgency ('Renewal: 2026-09-15 — Renewal soon') in a prominent amber-bordered div at the top of each policy card. Browser test verifies badge visibility and content at default viewport.

Cross-account API requests to /api/record/policy/2, /api/record/document/2 return HTTP 404 with {error:'Unavailable'} and no foreign policyholder names, policy details, or document data. Browser test verifies 404 status and absence of foreign data in response bodies.

After staff updates a request status to 'In review', policyholder signs back in and sees the updated 'In review' status text on the request without any notification mechanism. Browser test verifies the status change is visible after policyholder refresh.

Renewal urgency badge is positioned at the top of each policy card, above coverage details, document links, and request forms. Policyholders see renewal risk as their first decision before accessing other policy features. Browser test verifies badge visibility matches obligation-006.

Server-side ownership enforcement on all /api/record/* routes prevents direct URL access to another policyholder's policy, document, or service request. Returns generic 404 with no data disclosure. Browser test verifies via direct API requests with policyholder 1's session attempting policyholder 2's records.

The Harbor Point Insurance portal is implemented as a production-buildable Next.js application with proper TypeScript configuration, ESLint setup, and all required build/start/typecheck/lint/test scripts in package.json. The build command produces a deployable production bundle.

requirementClaims.implementationSummary: The portal is built for Harbor Point Insurance, an independent insurance broker, using fictional seeded policyholder and staff records in SQLite. Policyholders sign in and see only their own active policies, coverage summaries, renewal dates, and documents. Staff can review service requests and update statuses. Mobile access, privacy boundaries, keyboard navigation, and clear renewal urgency are prioritized. Claims adjudication, payments, and real carrier integrations are excluded.

Server-side ownership authorization in the /api/portal route filters policies, documents, and service requests by the authenticated user's id. A policyholder can never receive another policyholder's data from any API response. Cross-account isolation is verified in the Playwright browser test.

The Playwright test signs in as policyholder alex, verifies owned policies HP-1001 and HP-1002 are visible with coverage summaries, renewal dates with urgency labels, and document links, then confirms HP-2001 (owned by jordan) is absent. The policyholder opens a document link and returns to the dashboard.

After viewing policies, the policyholder selects a policy from the dropdown, describes needed help, and submits a service request. The portal confirms the request appears in the service requests list. After staff updates the status, the policyholder signs back in and sees the updated status and status history.

Staff user sam signs in and sees the Request review section with all submitted service requests. Staff can change the status dropdown to update a request. The Playwright test verifies the staff view is displayed and the status update persists.

All interactive elements (sign-in form, policy cards, document links, service request form, sign out button) use semantic HTML with labels, enabling full keyboard-only navigation. The visible focus indicator (3px amber outline) guides keyboard users through the entire workflow.

When a policyholder with multiple active policies is signed in, only their owned policies are returned by the server-side query. The UI displays all of the authenticated user's policies without showing any unrelated records from other policyholders.

The design uses a calm navy palette (#123b5d) with amber urgency accents (#b45b00), placing renewal attention first in a highlighted section, followed by active policy cards, then service requests. Mobile-first single-column layout expands to two columns on wider screens. Touch targets meet 44px minimum. Focus indicators are visible and logical.

The Playwright browser test performs cross-account verification: after signing in as alex, it asserts that jordan's policy HP-2001 has zero occurrences on the page. Server-side queries enforce owner=userId filtering on policies, documents, and service requests.

Each policy displays an urgency label (Urgent, Upcoming, or Later) as bold text alongside the renewal date. The Renewal attention section groups all policies with their urgency labels. Labels use text, not color alone. Focus indicators and semantic markup ensure keyboard accessibility.

Service requests store a JSON history array of status transitions with timestamps. The policyholder view displays status history as a progression (e.g., Received → In review). Staff status updates append to the history, and policyholders see the full progression on their next visit.

Sign-in uses seeded fictional usernames (alex, jordan, sam) validated against the SQLite users table. The access value is checked against FOUNDRY_RUNTIME_ACCESS_VALUE environment variable. No real identity provider is integrated. A launch checklist notes this is development-only access.

The urgency() function in lib/db.ts calculates days until renewal: <60 days = Urgent, <180 days = Upcoming, otherwise Later. These labels are displayed as bold text alongside the date in both the Renewal attention section and individual policy cards.

Server-side ownership filtering ensures policyholder API responses contain only policies where owner matches the authenticated user's id. The GET handler returns policies and requests scoped to the user. POST validates policy ownership before creating a request. PATCH restricts status updates to staff role only.

The service request form allows policyholders to select an owned policy and describe needed help. On submission, the server creates a request with Received status and a history entry. The policyholder sees the request in their list. After staff updates the status, the policyholder sees the updated status and history on reload.

Staff users see the Request review section with a status dropdown for each request. Policyholders never see staff controls; the role-based conditional rendering shows either CustomerView or StaffView. The PATCH endpoint rejects non-staff users. The Playwright test verifies 'My active policies' is absent in the staff view.

Renewal dates are displayed with explicit Urgent, Upcoming, or Later labels as bold text. The Renewal attention section uses a left border and background for visual distinction without relying on color alone. Labels are rendered as text content accessible to screen readers and keyboard users.

The project uses TypeScript with strict mode enabled. All files use proper type annotations including interfaces for database rows and component props. The typecheck script runs tsc --noEmit to verify clean compilation.

package.json defines the certified Next.js 15.4.4 stack with all required dependencies. The build script runs next build for production output. The start script runs next start. All source files are valid TypeScript/TSX that compile without errors.

requirementClaims.implementationSummary: The original customer request is fully implemented: three fictional practitioners, four services with different durations, working hours, existing appointments seeded in SQLite; customers choose a service, see filtered available practitioners and times, book with name and email, get on-screen confirmation; staff view the daily schedule and cancel bookings; local persistence with double-booking prevention; phone-first responsive layout; no external calendar or payment integration.

The business timezone 'Pacific Time (America/Los_Angeles)' is displayed on every booking view (data-testid booking-timezone), on each time slot button, on the booking confirmation (data-testid confirm-tz), and on the staff schedule view (data-testid schedule-timezone).

Customer selects a service showing duration, picks a date, sees filtered practitioners and time slots labeled with timezone, enters name and email, submits, and sees a confirmation page with service, practitioner, time, timezone, and name.

Staff navigates to /staff, views the daily schedule with timezone labels, selects an active appointment, confirms cancellation via a two-step button flow, and sees the booking marked as 'Cancelled' with distinct styling.

Booking confirmation is saved to localStorage and the appointment is persisted in SQLite. On page refresh, the confirmation reloads from localStorage and the SQLite record persists for the staff schedule.
When the customer changes the selected service, the date, practitioner list, and time slot selections are all reset so no stale choices remain.
If a selected time becomes unavailable (409 response), the API returns an error message displayed inline, and the customer can select a different time slot.
The staff schedule shows both active and cancelled appointments for a given day, with cancelled ones styled with a pink background and a 'Cancelled' label.

The design uses a calm, welcoming color palette (soft green #4d7958, neutral background #f6faf5), a single focused booking column on phones with large touch-friendly buttons (min-height 48px), progressive disclosure through numbered steps, and a compact staff daily view. Reversible cancellation uses a two-step confirm flow.
Each service button displays its name and duration in minutes (e.g., 'Swedish Massage — 60 min'). Duration is visible before the customer selects a date or time slot.

The booking API endpoint uses a SQLite transaction that rechecks for existing active appointments at the same practitioner, date, and overlapping time interval before inserting. If a conflict exists, it returns 0 and the endpoint responds with HTTP 409.

The constant TZ = 'Pacific Time (America/Los_Angeles)' is returned by every API response and displayed in the booking timezone header, each time slot button, the confirmation view, and the staff schedule timezone header.

Cancelled appointments appear in the staff schedule with a pink background (#fee) and a bold 'Cancelled' label (data-testid status-{id}). The cancel button is replaced by the status text, providing immediate visual evidence.
Staff access the schedule via the /staff route, which is a fixed fictional path with no authentication. A link from the customer booking page provides navigation.
The booking form collects only name and email via two input fields with aria labels. No additional fields are collected. Email validation uses a regex pattern.
After staff cancel a booking, the schedule reloads and the cancelled booking remains visible with a distinct pink background and 'Cancelled' label, persisting across page refreshes.

Service selection shows four services with durations. Clicking a service enables date selection. Choosing a date fetches filtered practitioners and time slots for that service. Only practitioners linked to the selected service with available slots on that day are shown.

After entering name and email and clicking 'Confirm booking', the API atomically rechecks availability within a SQLite transaction and creates the appointment. The confirmation screen shows service, duration, practitioner, date, time with timezone, and customer name. The booking persists in SQLite and localStorage survives refresh. Customer email is not displayed on the confirmation screen to avoid unnecessary exposure.

The SQLite transaction in the POST handler checks for any existing active appointment at the same practitioner, date, and overlapping time before inserting. If found, it returns HTTP 409. The Playwright test verifies this by attempting a duplicate booking via fetch and asserting a 409 status.

The /staff page shows appointments for a selected day. Each active appointment has a 'Cancel' button that reveals a 'Yes, cancel' confirmation button. Clicking it sends a POST to cancel the appointment, reloads the schedule, and shows the 'Cancelled' status label.

All data is stored in a SQLite database at data/juniper.db. Seed data (practitioners, services, links, hours, one existing appointment) is inserted on first run. Appointments created or cancelled persist across application restarts and page refreshes.

The booking flow uses a single-column layout with max-width 520px, full-width buttons with min-height 48px for touch targets, 16px font size inputs, and proper box-sizing. The Playwright test verifies no horizontal overflow at 375px width.

The timezone string 'Pacific Time (America/Los_Angeles)' appears in the booking page header (data-testid booking-timezone), on each time slot button, on the confirmation page (data-testid confirm-tz), and in the staff schedule header (data-testid schedule-timezone). The Playwright test verifies both customer and staff views contain the timezone.

The project uses Next.js 15.4.4 with TypeScript, includes package.json with build/start/typecheck/lint/test scripts, tsconfig.json, eslint.config.mjs with FlatCompat and .next ignore, app/layout.tsx root layout, /api/health endpoint returning 200, and public/icon.svg favicon.

Customers choose a service, see only available practitioners and times, book with name and email, and receive an on-screen confirmation. Staff can view the daily schedule and cancel a booking. Persist appointments locally, prevent double-booking, and make the customer flow excellent on phones. No external calendar or payment integration yet.

requirementClaims.implementationSummary: Built a complete multi-staff appointment booking app for Juniper Wellness Studio with SQLite persistence, three fictional practitioners, four duration-specific services, working hours, existing seed appointments, customer booking flow, and staff schedule with cancellation.
Every booking view and staff schedule view shows the operating timezone label 'Pacific Time (PT)' via data-testid attributes booking-timezone, review-tz, conf-tz, and staff-timezone.

Customer selects a service, picks a date, sees only compatible practitioners with available time slots filtered by service duration and existing bookings. Slot buttons are organized by practitioner with working-hour constraints applied.

After selecting a time slot, the customer enters name and email, advances to a review step showing service, duration, practitioner, date, time with timezone, name, and email, then confirms to receive an on-screen booking confirmation.

Staff schedule page at /staff shows practitioner-grouped daily appointments with timezone label, allows cancellation via per-appointment cancel buttons, and displays CANCELLED status distinctly from ACTIVE status.
When a customer changes service selection they return to step 1, and choosing a new service resets practitioner/time selections and recalculates availability from scratch for the new duration.
Back buttons in the review and details steps preserve the customer's entered name and email values in React state, so navigating backward does not lose entered details.
Staff can refresh the schedule page and appointments persist because all data is stored in SQLite. The Playwright test verifies appointment count survives page.reload().

Calm, phone-first design with single-column layout (max-width 480px for booking, 700px for staff), generous touch targets, progressive disclosure through 5 steps, sticky navigation, botanical color scheme (#3a6b4f accents), white cards with subtle shadows, and compact practitioner-grouped staff schedule rows.
A dedicated review step (step 4 of 5) displays service name with duration, practitioner name, date and time range with timezone, customer name, and email before the final confirm button.
Cancelled appointments remain visible in the staff schedule table with CANCELLED status text in red, reduced opacity, and the cancel button hidden. Active appointments show green ACTIVE status.
All data is stored in a single local SQLite database at data/juniper.db using better-sqlite3 with WAL journal mode. No external calendar integration or multi-instance synchronization.
Customers provide only name and email to complete a booking. No accounts, authentication, or payment fields are included.

Available practitioners are filtered by practitioner_services join for the selected service. Time slots are generated in 30-minute increments within each practitioner's working hours, excluding slots that overlap existing active appointments for that practitioner on the selected date. Duration-specific filtering ensures the slot plus service duration fits within working hours.

Customer submits name and email, which are validated client-side and server-side (regex for email, non-empty name). On successful POST to /api/appointments returning 201, the confirmation step displays all appointment details.

Appointments are persisted in SQLite. The GET /api/appointments endpoint retrieves all appointments from the database. After page refresh, the same data is loaded from the persistent store. The Playwright test verifies count survives reload.

The POST /api/appointments endpoint performs a conflict check query: SELECT id FROM appointments WHERE practitioner_id=? AND date=? AND status='active' AND start_time < ? AND end_time > ? (overlap detection). If a conflict exists, it returns HTTP 409 with an error message. The Playwright test verifies this by attempting a duplicate booking.

The /staff page shows all appointments grouped by practitioner for a selected date. Each active appointment has a Cancel button that PATCHes /api/appointments/[id] with status:'cancelled'. The appointment row then shows CANCELLED in red with reduced opacity, and the cancel button disappears.

Database initialization seeds 3 practitioners (Sage Thornberry 9-17, Rowan Blackwell 10-18, Fern Whitmore 8-16), 4 services (Guided Relaxation 30min, Deep Tissue Bodywork 60min, Herbal Consultation 45min, Extended Renewal Session 90min), practitioner-service associations, and 3 existing appointments on 2025-01-15.

The booking page header shows 'All times shown in Pacific Time (PT)' via data-testid='booking-timezone'. The review step shows the timezone. The confirmation shows it via data-testid='conf-tz'. The staff schedule shows it via data-testid='staff-timezone'. The timezone constant is defined in lib/db.ts.

Package.json includes build script running 'next build'. TypeScript configuration, ESLint configuration with .next ignore, proper App Router layout, and all type annotations ensure successful production build.

requirementClaims.implementationSummary: The original customer request is implemented as a complete multi-staff appointment booking application for Juniper Wellness Studio with three fictional practitioners, four services with different durations, working hours, seeded existing appointments, customer service-first booking with name and email, on-screen confirmation, staff daily schedule, cancellation, local SQLite persistence, double-booking prevention, and phone-first design. No external calendar or payment integration.
Every booking and schedule view displays the studio timezone (America/Denver) as a visible label via the tz-label, conf-timezone, and staff-tz test IDs.
The booking page implements a progressive funnel: customer selects service, sees filtered practitioners and times, enters name and email, submits, and sees confirmation with all details and timezone.
The staff page loads the daily schedule with timezone label, displays all appointments, and provides a cancel button that updates the appointment to cancelled status while retaining the record.
Appointments are persisted to SQLite. After booking and page refresh, the appointment remains in the database and appears on the staff schedule.
When a customer selects a different service, the availability recalculates with the new duration, showing only valid practitioners and times for the newly selected service.

When a slot is taken during submission, the API returns a 409 error with a user-friendly message. The customer's name and email remain in the form fields so they can choose another slot without re-entering details.
The staff schedule API returns all appointments for a date including both seeded and newly created ones, joined with practitioner and service names.

The design uses a calm juniper green palette, phone-first vertical booking funnel with progress indicators, generous touch targets, persistent labels, and a denser staff schedule. Progressive disclosure with inline validation and explicit confirmation.

The availability API calculates slots using 15-minute increments within each practitioner's working hours, filtering out any slot where the service duration would cause overlap with existing active appointments.

Cancellation updates the appointment status to 'cancelled' without deleting the record. The staff schedule shows cancelled appointments with italic 'Cancelled' text. Availability calculations exclude cancelled appointments.
The booking page uses a 3-step progress bar, large touch-friendly buttons, persistent form labels, inline validation errors, and a mobile-optimized 375px-first layout.
The availability API shows only practitioners and time slots where the selected service's duration fits within working hours without overlapping any active appointment.
The studio timezone (America/Denver) is displayed on the booking page timezone label, the confirmation screen, and the staff schedule page.
The cancel API updates appointment status to 'cancelled' rather than deleting. The availability API filters on status='active', so cancelled slots become available for rebooking.

The database seeds exactly 3 practitioners (Sage Oliveira, River Chen, Wren Patel) with distinct working hours, 4 services (Restorative Massage 60min, Guided Meditation 30min, Acupuncture Session 45min, Deep Tissue Therapy 90min), and 2 existing active appointments.
After selecting a service, the page fetches filtered availability showing only practitioners and time slots that can accommodate the service duration without overlap.

The book API validates name and email, rechecks for overlapping active appointments before inserting, and returns 409 on conflict. The Playwright test verifies both successful creation and overlap rejection.
The confirmation screen displays service name, practitioner name, date, time range, customer name, email, and timezone in a clear layout with the conf-timezone element showing America/Denver.
The staff page shows a timezone-labeled daily schedule. Cancellation updates the appointment to 'cancelled' status, shows italic 'Cancelled' text, persists across refresh, and releases the time slot.

The booking flow uses a 375px mobile viewport with progress bar, persistent labels for name and email, inline validation errors for missing/invalid fields, and recoverable form state. The Playwright test runs at 375x812 viewport.

Cancelled appointments remain in the database with status='cancelled'. The availability API excludes cancelled appointments from overlap checks, allowing the released slot to be rebooked. The Playwright test verifies this flow.

The Next.js TypeScript application is configured with proper tsconfig.json, next.config.mjs with serverExternalPackages for better-sqlite3, and package.json build script for successful production builds.

requirementClaims.implementationSummary: Full application implements multi-staff appointment booking with three fictional practitioners (Maya Rivera, Eli Thornton, Suki Patel), four services with different durations (60, 45, 30, 90 min), Mon-Fri 9-5 working hours, and two seeded demo appointments. Customer booking flow with service selection, date picking, duration-aware availability, name/email collection, review, and confirmation. Staff daily schedule view with date navigation and two-step cancellation. SQLite persistence with transactional conflict-safe booking. Visible timezone (America/Los_Angeles) on all views. Demo banner labels fictional data. Phone-first responsive design with grouped touch targets.
Timezone label (America/Los_Angeles) displayed on booking flow, review card, confirmation section, and staff schedule view via TimezoneTag component with data-testid timezone-label.

Step-by-step customer flow: select service (step 0), choose date (step 1), pick available practitioner and time slot (step 2), enter name/email and review with timezone (step 3), submit and see confirmation (step 4).

Staff Schedule view with date picker loads appointments grouped by practitioner. Cancel button triggers confirmation dialog (Yes, Cancel / No), then removes appointment from active schedule via cancelled=1 update.
Booking API uses SQLite transaction with conflict check: SELECT for overlapping active appointments before INSERT. Returns 409 with error message if conflict exists, preventing duplicate bookings.
Selecting a new service resets date, practitioner, and time selections. Going back from date step returns to service selection with clean state via resetBooking and step navigation.
Staff schedule reloads from SQLite on date change and after cancellation, showing current persisted state including cancelled status changes.

Calm wellness aesthetic with soft botanical colors (#00b894 juniper green, #f8f7f4 background), generous spacing, stacked cards for services, grouped time buttons, sequential low-density customer flow, medium-density staff rows, Back/Continue navigation, and demo banner.

Booking creation wrapped in db.transaction() that checks for overlapping appointments (start_time < endTime AND end_time > startTime AND cancelled=0) before inserting. Returns 409 conflict error if overlap found.
Demo banner with warning icon visible on all views. Practitioners labeled (fictional) in availability and schedule. Seed appointments marked fictional=1 and shown as (demo) in staff view.

Time slots displayed as wrapped button groups with max 12 visible per practitioner (with +N more indicator). Touch targets minimum 44px. Phone viewport tested at 375x667 for overflow, bounded choices, and reasonable height.
Single Next.js application with better-sqlite3 database stored in data/juniper.db. Lazy initialization on first API call. WAL journal mode. All data shared between customer and staff views.
Four-step customer booking flow: service cards → date buttons → practitioner/time groups → review/confirm form. Back navigation at each step. Single column layout with maxWidth 600px.

Three practitioners (Maya Rivera, Eli Thornton, Suki Patel) with fictional=1, four services (60/45/30/90 min), Mon-Fri 9-17 working hours, two seed appointments on next Monday. Demo banner identifies all as fictional demonstration data.

get_availability API filters practitioners by service via practitioner_services join, checks working_hours for selected day_of_week, generates 15-min interval slots checking duration fit within working hours, and excludes slots overlapping any active appointment.

Book action validates name and email (non-empty, contains @), creates appointment in transaction, returns appointment details with practitioner, service, and timezone. Confirmation section displays all fields including timezone label.
SQLite database in data/ directory persists across restarts. Transactional booking with conflict SELECT before INSERT prevents double-booking. Browser test verifies persistence and conflict behavior.
Staff Schedule view loads appointments by date with practitioner grouping. Cancel button shows Yes/Cancel confirmation. Confirmed cancellation sets cancelled=1 and reloads schedule showing removal.

MaxWidth 600px container, stacked service cards, wrapped date/time buttons with min 44px touch targets, sequential steps with Back navigation, slots capped at 12 per group, timezone visible, aria-labels on all interactive controls. Tested at 375x667 viewport for no horizontal overflow, bounded choices, and reasonable scroll height.
TimezoneTag component renders America/Los_Angeles timezone on booking flow header, review card, confirmation section, and staff schedule view. Same TIMEZONE constant used throughout API responses.
All source files written in TypeScript with strict mode. Types defined for Practitioner, Service, Appointment, WorkingHour interfaces. Component props and state properly typed.
Standard Next.js App Router structure with package.json build script, next.config.mjs, tsconfig.json, and eslint.config.mjs. All routes use proper exports for GET/POST handlers.

initial.originalPrompt: Build a multi-staff appointment booking application for Juniper Wellness Studio. requirementClaims.implementationSummary: Built a multi-staff appointment booking application for Juniper Wellness Studio with three seeded practitioners, four services with different durations, working hours, existing appointments, customer booking with name and email, on-screen confirmation, staff daily schedule with cancellation, local SQLite persistence, double-booking prevention, and phone-first design.
Every booking view and staff schedule view shows a visible timezone badge displaying America/Los_Angeles so staff and customers interpret times consistently.

Customer selects a service, date, practitioner, and available time through progressive guided steps, enters name and email, submits, and reads confirmation containing service, practitioner, date, time, and timezone.

Staff opens a date-specific schedule, scans appointments grouped by practitioner, confirms cancellation with a deliberate two-step flow, and sees retained cancelled history plus released availability.
When customer changes service after viewing availability, the practitioner and slot lists are re-fetched and filtered accordingly via useEffect dependencies.
After confirmation, a 'Book Another' button resets the booking flow so the customer can start another booking.
Staff schedule fetches from SQLite on date change or view switch, showing locally persisted active and cancelled appointments that survive page refresh.

Design uses quiet juniper green (#4a7c59) with warm neutral surfaces (#f5f0eb), phone-first single-column layout with max-width 480px, progressive disclosure through guided steps, and practitioner-grouped staff schedule.
Phone customers progress through bounded service, date, practitioner, and time choices with step indicators, one decision per screen, and Next/Back navigation.
The POST /api/booking book action rechecks practitioner availability from existing active appointments immediately before inserting, rejecting with HTTP 409 on conflict.

Cancellation sets appointment status to 'cancelled' (retained in DB), the cancelled card remains visible with a visual indicator, and the getAvailableSlots function only considers 'active' appointments, releasing cancelled times.
Available slots are computed from working hours, service duration, and existing active appointments. Only genuinely available times are shown. The timezone is displayed alongside choices.
Cancelled bookings remain in the database with status 'cancelled', are displayed with a cancelled visual style on the staff schedule, and their time slots become available again for new bookings.

Customers choose a service from a labeled select, see only available practitioners for that service, see only available time slots computed from working hours minus active appointments, and submit name and email to book. The timezone badge is visible throughout.
Appointments are persisted in SQLite. The booking API performs a final overlap check against active appointments before INSERT, rejecting conflicts with HTTP 409. Data survives page refresh.
On successful booking, a confirmation card displays service name, practitioner name, date, start/end time, timezone (America/Los_Angeles), customer name, and email.

Staff view shows a date-selectable daily schedule grouped by practitioner. Active appointments have a Cancel Booking button with deliberate two-step confirmation. Cancelled records remain visible with a 'cancelled' status badge and visual styling. Released times reappear in customer availability.

Design uses phone-first single-column layout (max-width 480px), separate Book/Staff Schedule navigation with aria-label, labeled keyboard-accessible controls with visible focus indicators, progressive step-by-step disclosure, bounded slot groups, and no horizontal overflow. Playwright test verifies at 375px viewport.

The application is a Next.js 15.4.4 TypeScript project with proper package.json scripts (build, start, typecheck, lint, test), tsconfig.json, eslint.config.mjs, and App Router layout. Production build completes successfully.
